extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians, comedy critics, and comedy-interested readers
extracted.subtask_description: A short essay giving normative criteria for what counts as comedy versus 'anti-comedy' or 'meta-comedy', with examples (roast, Andy Kaufman, a moth joke) and value judgments about authenticity and technique. Useful for judging performers or understanding the authorial stance on comedic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer must find their own material funny (authenticity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every joke I’ve ever told I found funny at the time. Sometimes, looking back, I found them unfunny. But at the time, they made me laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity of the performer's reaction to their material is a criterion: if the performer genuinely finds a joke funny when delivering it, that supports it being comedy rather than a stunt or critique. Self-deception or retrospective re-evaluation doesn't negate the initial authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-comedy is not comedy but critique/ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth is all anti-comedy, or meta-comedy, is worthless. It is for the weak and cowardly... It is not comedy. It is critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a performance's primary mode is ridiculing other comedians or comedic forms rather than attempting to produce laughter as comedy, it should be judged as critique, not as comedy. Such work is viewed negatively by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-comics choose the worst on purpose and mock it
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea is this. The performer does not find the comedy he sees to be funny. So he chooses the worst he can find and ridicules it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately doing 'the worst' material as a statement (doing something 'intentionally bad') is identified as an anti-comedy tactic; evaluate this as a rhetorical/critical move rather than genuine comedic craft, and regard it as a weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally bad doesn't justify being bad (intent vs quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because, goes their thinking, 'intentionally bad is better than unintentionally bad I could argue either way on this but I know one thing. Both are bad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't excuse poor comedic quality simply because it is framed as intentional. Both intentionally bad and unintentionally bad material should be judged on whether it actually produces comedy; intentionality alone is not a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience laughter must be due to joke quality, not meta-commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: They did not laugh because it was a comment on bd jokes and how we all know they are bad. They laughed because it was a very good joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a joke, determine whether audience response stems from the joke's craftsmanship and funniness itself rather than from clever commentary about comedy or expectations. Good jokes produce real laughter independent of meta-angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual subversion (e.g., clean jokes at a roast) can be valid
rubrics_metrics.description: This is because my jokes were not dirty, but instead clean... I truly believed that doing clean jokes in this context would be shocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailoring content to context (choosing clean material where dirty is expected) can legitimately create shock or surprise and be a valid comedic technique, not necessarily an anti-comedy move. Evaluate such choices by their effect, not by a label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of genuine comedic techniques distinguishes great comics (Andy Kaufman example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Andy Kaufman was a comic. He used comedic techniques, he ridiculed no comedic techniques... Andy Kaufman was one of the greatest comics ever, because of his large arsenal of comedic weapons, which he only used when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality coupled with mastery of comedic techniques is a positive criterion. A performer who deploys a coherent set of comedic tools to produce effects (rather than merely to bewilder or to mock) should be judged as a true comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-comics tend to appeal to critics rather than the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-comics, when you come right down to it are critics, which may be why they find favor among, guess who, critics... He was misunderstood by a small minority who were convinced he was misunderstood by the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whom the act is designed to please: if it primarily seeks critical approval or signals understanding to a niche, that is indicative of anti-comic positioning rather than broad comedic success. Popular audience reaction is a separate metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridiculing the art you love is a disqualifying stance
rubrics_metrics.description: I am a comic and these (anti-comics and meta-comics) are my enemies... I am a comic and therefor despise anyone who ridicules what I love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A normatively prescriptive criterion: treating the artform itself with ridicule—rather than engaging with it to produce laughter—is presented as a betrayal of comic values and grounds for negative judgment of the performer.
